Interactive IRT teaching labs

Source: R/labs.R
run_lab.Rd

mirtverse ships interactive learnr tutorials for measurement courses. Students work through a realistic testing scenario with live R exercises and make the decisions an analyst would make, getting feedback on each one. Labs 1 and 2 share one storyline, a certification board's 32-item exam (certexam). Labs 3 to 11 each have their own: A provincial numeracy test (numeracy), a licensure exam with two forms (linking), a placement test's item bank (catbank), rater-scored science tasks (openended), written science explanations (essays), the text of numeracy items (itemtext), a field test of generated items (aigfield), an AI-scored science test (aiscored) and a fractions test with its knowledge graph (fractions).

Usage

run_lab(name = "model-choice", ...)

list_labs()

Arguments

name

the lab to run; see list_labs().

...

passed to learnr::run_tutorial(), for example shiny_args = list(launch.browser = FALSE).

Value

list_labs() returns a data frame with one row per lab: name, title and description. run_lab() runs the lab and returns nothing useful.

Details

  • "model-choice" (Lab 1): Score the responses, screen the items, check dimensionality, compare the Rasch, 2PL and 3PL models, check item fit and local dependence, and commit to a model the board can defend.

  • "decisions" (Lab 2): Read the item parameters, check precision at the pass mark, choose a scoring method, estimate classification accuracy, test for DIF between English and French candidates, write a memo, and compare the results with the truth behind the data.

  • "fairness" (Lab 3): Is a numeracy test biased against English language learners? Separate impact from DIF, run Mantel-Haenszel and IRT likelihood-ratio DIF tests, purify the anchor, judge how much the DIF matters for students' scores and plan a content review.

  • "linking" (Lab 4): A licensure exam's pass rate jumped on a new form. Calibrate both forms, link them through common items, catch a drifted anchor, compare separate and concurrent calibration, and carry the pass mark over with IRT true-score equating.

  • "cat-design" (Lab 5): Could a computerized adaptive test replace a 40-item placement test? Inspect the item bank, run a CAT by hand, simulate students, and choose a stopping rule, exposure control and content balancing.

  • "open-ended" (Lab 6): Are the rubric scores on a science assessment trustworthy? Check rater agreement, find a severe and an inconsistent rater, resolve final scores, fit polytomous IRT models, collapse categories that do not work, and decide whether an automated scoring engine can replace a human reader.

  • "auto-scoring" (Lab 7): Can an automated scoring engine score written science explanations on its own? Train an engine with train_scorer(), judge it on new students with agreement_report(), check it for English language learners, find what drives the difference, and choose the engine's role.

  • "item-text" (Lab 8): Can item difficulty be predicted from the text before field testing? Describe items with item_features(), find near-duplicates and miskeyed items, compare an LLTM with a lasso and a random forest in predict_difficulty(), catch a leaky feature, hold out whole item models, and decide what predictions can replace.

  • "aig" (Lab 9): Can a family mean replace the field test of a generated item? Write an item model with item_model() and fix its constraints, calibrate a field test of 60 isomorphs, find the families that are not isomorphic with calibrate_families() and why, and test the family means on held-out items.

  • "ai-audit" (Lab 10): Can the scores of an AI-scored test be released? Audit the engine with ai_audit(): Agreement with human raters, bias against English language learners, drift after an engine update and DIF on the test as scored; then draft a validity argument with validity_argument() and decide which scores to report.

  • "kg-repair" (Lab 11): Is a curriculum team's knowledge graph right before diagnostic reports are built on it? Check its structure with mv_kg_check(), check it against the answers with mv_kg_fit(), find an item linked to the wrong concept and a missing prerequisite, repair the graph with mv_kg_refine(), and show what the repair changes for mastery patterns and item difficulty (mv_kg_explain()).

run_lab() opens a lab in the browser (or the RStudio Viewer). The labs also appear in RStudio's Tutorial pane once mirtverse and learnr are installed. Progress is saved in the browser, so students can stop and come back later.

Examples

list_labs()
#> # A tibble: 11 × 3
#>    name         title                                             description   
#>    <chr>        <chr>                                             <chr>         
#>  1 ai-audit     Lab 10: Auditing an AI-scored test                A state scien…
#>  2 aig          Lab 9: Building an item factory                   A numeracy pr…
#>  3 auto-scoring Lab 7: Can the engine score alone?                A science pro…
#>  4 cat-design   Lab 5: Designing an adaptive test                 A college wan…
#>  5 decisions    Lab 2: From parameters to decisions               The certifica…
#>  6 fairness     Lab 3: Is the test fair? Detecting DIF            An advocacy g…
#>  7 item-text    Lab 8: Predicting difficulty before field testing A numeracy pr…
#>  8 kg-repair    Lab 11: Repairing a knowledge graph               A district's …
#>  9 linking      Lab 4: Linking two forms                          A licensure e…
#> 10 model-choice Lab 1: Choosing a model the board can defend      You are the n…
#> 11 open-ended   Lab 6: Scoring open-ended responses               A science ass…
if (interactive()) run_lab("model-choice")
